messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur is a 74-year-old retired combat pilot, a man whose life was once defined by precision, discipline, and the calculated management of risk. For years after his wife passed, he lived a quiet, orderly life in the small town where he’d settled after his service. That order shattered two years ago. The relationship with his new partner, which began as a welcome antidote to loneliness, had descended into a private world of unpredictable violence, almost always fueled by the sharp, cloying smell of whiskey on her breath. The trauma was not a single event but a campaign of domestic terror, ending only when he finally found the will to make her leave. He believed that with her gone, the threat was over. He was wrong.

The sense of being under constant threat became a permanent feature of his existence, a low-frequency hum of dread that never fully subsided. At night, Arthur finds it nearly impossible to fall asleep; he lies awake for hours, convinced he needs to remain alert, listening for any sound that might signal an intrusion. This pervasive feeling of being unsafe has dictated the rules of his new life. In response to this constant hypervigilance, he has systematically dismantled his social connections, believing that emotional closeness is a liability he can no longer afford. He avoids intimacy with his children and grandchildren, keeping conversations brief and deflecting any attempts at deeper connection. He has also made a rigid vow to himself to never allow the simmering rage inside him to surface, certain that expressing it would make him monstrous, just like her.

These strategies are reinforced whenever he encounters the world outside his home. A trip to the local VFW hall, a place he once considered a sanctuary, became an ordeal when an old friend clapped him firmly on the shoulder. The unexpected physical touch sent a jolt of panic through him, his heart hammering against his ribs. The smell of alcohol from the bar was the final straw. He fled without a word, his flight solidifying his belief that avoidance is his only tool for survival. Anything that reminds him of her—the sight of her car, the brand of whiskey she drank, even a woman with a similar laugh—sends him into retreat, further entrenching his isolation.

His self-imposed solitude, meant to protect him, has ironically made him more vulnerable. By avoiding any cues related to his former partner, his world has shrunk to the point where any potential reminder feels catastrophic. A chance sighting of her across the street while getting his mail is no longer a minor annoyance but a full-blown activation of his threat system, leaving him trembling and breathless. His strategy of avoiding perpetrator cues has paradoxically made those very cues more potent when they inevitably appear, turning his small town into a minefield.

Furthermore, the very strategies he uses to manage his fear end up amplifying it. The quiet hours he spends alone, avoiding others, provide fertile ground for his hypervigilance to grow. In the silence of his house, every creak of the floorboards is a potential intruder, every shadow a lurking figure. The anger he works so hard to suppress churns within him, creating a feeling of internal pressure that is itself a source of threat. He feels like a machine with no safety valve, constantly on the verge of breaking. This internal state of high alert is a direct consequence of the isolation and suppression he relies on for safety, a vicious cycle where his solution has become the engine of his distress. Arthur finally sought therapy after receiving a wedding invitation from his eldest granddaughter. The thought of being in a crowded church, of the requisite hugs and handshakes, of the champagne toasts, felt like an impossible demand. He realized his carefully constructed fortress had become a prison, and he was terrified that he would lose his family completely if he could not find a way to walk out of it.
